utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, everyone. Is there anything to be raised before we hear evidence? Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Good afternoon. This relates to the next witness and the protective measures which are to be granted to the witness, and I would like to make my remarks in public session and I'll keep them general because it's a matter of a principle as opposed to something that will reveal the identity of the witness. So, first of all, we want to again reiterate that we object to closed-session testimony in this trial unless it's absolutely necessary. And we note that in this case the witness had testified in the first trial here at the Tribunal without closed session, and so we think that he ought to be, at the minimum, asked whether or not his subsequent requesting of a closed session was generic to the particular case that he was testifying in and whether he needs to have the testimony in this case in closed session where there's an absolute record of no problem that any of our witnesses who've testified in this case have had. We think the Chamber ought to make as many efforts as possible to have this testimony heard in public --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Robinson. You knew from the beginning that this witness is given the protection of closed session a while ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is this something we should spend time, precious time, court time? Could it not have been -- have been raised in writing in advance?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Every time we've raised something like this in writing, however, you've declined to inquire as to the witness, so we decided that it's better to just ask you before the witness comes in rather than starting a motion with an answer and a written decision, because you've, in the past and as recently as last week, declined to inquire of the witnesses whether or not the protective measures that they have in place should be continued. And I'm referring to your decision on protective measures for KDZ-601 and 605, which I believe was issued on the 18th of August. So we didn't believe that it would be a good idea to raise the same issue in writing, but nevertheless, I apologise for taking your time, but I think it's an important principle that we would like to maintain each time a witness comes here. I also wanted to point out to the Chamber that if you Google the name of this witness, you'll find newspaper articles about the very same thing that he's going to testify about, and so to us these protective measures seem really unnecessary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Elliott, would you like to respond?

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As the Court has noted, the details surrounding this witness's protective measures were contained in the 4th of July notification. And unless the Court wants me to, I won't bother revisiting the circumstances surrounding these protective measures, but this Trial Chamber has repeatedly held and most notably on the 14th of September, 2010, decision, that it doesn't need to hear personally from a witness when considering a request to modify or rescind existing protective measures where certain circumstances exist, and they existed here. So I submit it's unnecessary to hear from this witness regarding his protective measure status.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber sees no reason to -- to vary the protective measures allowed to the witness by the previous Chambers. Yes, Ms. Elliott. Shall we go into private session to bring in the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: Just one matter, Your Honour. It relates to Exhibit D1585. And a revised translation was ordered for this exhibit on the 19th of July, 2011, and that's been received and has now been uploaded in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Unless there's anything, we'll go into private session -- I'm sorry, closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. If you could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Ms. Edgerton, before you begin, I wanted to tell you that we'll have another break, a last break for the day at 10 to 6.00 for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Then could you give us your full name.

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Musan Talovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Talovic, if you could look at me. Thank you. Mr. Talovic, do you remember 11 years ago in June of 2000 and then again in 2002 giving statements to investigators from the Office of the Prosecutor for this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And those statements were about what happened to you in Glogova in May of 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And then do you remember in 2004 giving a statement to the cantonal prosecutor's office in Tuzla about the same thing?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in July of this year, 2011, in Sarajevo, do you remember signing another statement putting all those earlier statements together into one document?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And did you look at that statement from 2011 before you came to testify here today?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you noticed a problem with the handwritten date on the first page, didn't you? It says 2001, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I should have added another 1 there, yes. I did it personally.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Talovic, when you answer my questions and Dr. Karadzic's later on, you are going to have to lean forward a little bit more than you are and speak into the microphones with the red lights on, in front of you, okay? Great. Thank you. Now, Mr. Talovic, other than that little correction, are you satisfied that the statement you signed in July of 2011 is accurate as far as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if you were asked the same questions that you were asked in 2000, 2002, 2004, and July of this year, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: The same, all of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, then, Your Honours, could I offer the -- or tender the amalgamated statement of Mr. Talovic, 65 ter 90261, as the next Prosecution exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3188, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll now read a summary of that written evidence. Up until 9 May 1992, Musan Talovic had lived his whole life in the village of Glogova in the municipality of Bratunac. In April 1992, tensions in the area rose. The witness recalls the police was divided into Serb and Muslim sections. And April 1st, Serb police went through the area, calling for people to surrender their weapons at the Bratunac municipality building. On April 3rd, villagers from nearby Hranca fled to Glogova reporting that local Chetniks were burning houses and killing people. Early in the morning of 9 May, Mr. Talovic woke to find haystacks burning around the village and soldiers coming toward them. Muslim men from the area gathered at his house and tried to hide near a creek close by. They were found by armed Serbs in uniform, one of whom the witness recognised. Their captors directed the prisoners at gunpoint to the supermarket in the village centre. The witness saw numbers of Serb soldiers gathered nearby. Eventually Najdan Mladjenovic arrived. He directed three of the Muslim prisoners into his car. The witness then heard Mladjenovic issue orders to get on with the job and kill the rest. Four of the soldiers came forward armed with automatic weapons. They took the remaining 20 men, including the witness, to the riverbank where they were ordered to line up and face the river. The soldiers opened fire on the group. The witness hit the water and lost consciousness. He woke hours later 10 metres downstream under a tree and two dead bodies. He recognised the bodies. They were his neighbours. The witness found only one survivor to the shooting who had been wounded trying to escape. The rest of the prisoners were killed. In the village, Mr. Talovic saw houses burning and found the bodies of more neighbours who had also been killed that day. Altogether, there was a total of 68 victims of the Serb attack. That night the witness and other survives of the attack decided to leave the village of Glogova. One group made their way to Konjevic Polje, another to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Talovic, I just have a few clarifying questions about the written evidence that I've just read a summary of. First of all, in that written evidence in paragraph 8, you mention that Miroslav Deronjic was the main person on the Serbian Crisis Staff. How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Because Selim Delic and Nesib Besovic [phoen] went to negotiate in Bratunac and they returned and told us that Miomir Nikolic and Miroslav Deronjic were the main people on that Crisis Staff of the SDS of the Serb Republic in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Talovic, on the 9th of May, did you see any military vehicles in Glogova?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: I saw a APC and a tank in the centre of Glogova when we were brought there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Were there any personnel manning those pieces of military equipment?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Three or four men were on the APC. They were armed with a PAM and a machine-gun and a tank - you know what that is - and there were other soldiers accompanying them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Military uniforms, olive-green/grey.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you mean when you describe a PAM?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what is mounted on an APC, and it turns around, and I think it has these big bullets, and they kept twirling it around and scaring us.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you see any markings of any kind on the transporter or the tank?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now to move on, in paragraph 31 of your statement, you describe how Mustafa Golic, Sejid Ibisevic, and Almaz Talovic were taken away in Najdan Mladjenovic's car, but later on, in paragraphs 39 and 40, you describe how you met with Golic again and what he told you. So I'd like to know after they were taken away did you ever see Ibisevic and Talovic again?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Talovic is my cousin and Sejid is a neighbour. They were killed that same night. And Mustafa Golic is alive to this day. He survived. He managed to run away. How he managed to do that, that is what he knows. From the school of Vuk Karadzic, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How do you know that Sejid Ibisevic and Almaz Talovic were killed the same night?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Well, because these neighbours when we met up later on, they said they were buried in Voljevica. The graves are there, and they know to this day who found them and who buried them. And this is my very own cousin. I asked about him.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, to move on, in paragraph 35 of your statement, you list a number of names, including yourself, of men who you say were lined up with you at the edge of the river. Now, apart from yourself and the three men who you said were taken away by car whose names also appear in that list and Seco Delic, who you refer to later in your statement, to your knowledge did any of these men in that list at paragraph 35 survive this shooting?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: None of them survived excepted myself and Seco Delic, who was later killed by a shell.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you just repeat the end of your sentence that you've just given, the answer where you said Seco Delic was killed by a shell. The interpreter didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: It was later, five or six or seven months later. Seco was just wounded. He survived.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Among the victims, among the group that was with you and shot on the side of the riverbank, were there any children?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Hajrem [phoen] Ibisevic was 11 and Mujo Ibisevic was 13. The rest were 18, 20, young men.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, to your knowledge, up until this time, till the 9th of May, had any of these victims been involved in any kind of military activity whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: None of them ever. They never participated in any such thing or did they have any need to.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, later on in your statement you give another list of names at paragraph 38 where you describe how after the shooting you saw the bodies of killed persons from your village which had been piled in two locations. There are 24 people listed there. Now, can you just clarify because it's not perfectly clear in your statement, are those 24 people the names of some of the villagers you saw who had been killed and whose bodies had been piled up?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: All of them are neighbours, all of these men there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Were they all men, those 24 who you saw?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: All of them except Banovka and Adem.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you just repeat your sentence. You said "All of them except Banovka and Adem," what?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Junuzovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And who was Adem Junuzovic?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Banovka's husband.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And can I just -- I'll go back to line 11 at page 63 and correct myself. You saw actually far more than 24 bodies, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, just another question about these lists at paragraph 35 and paragraph 38. The name Selmo Omerovic -- pardon me the name Selmo Omerovic appears on both lists. How could that be?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Selmo Omerovic, father's name Hakija; Selmo Omerovic, father's name Adem. These are two different men, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now on this list in paragraph 38, I saw the name Uzeir Talovic. Is he any relation to you?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: That's my father's side of the family, children of my uncle.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And one last question: How did this experience, even though it's many years after the fact -- how did this experience of being shot down and then surviving affect you?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: My neighbours and my family know better than anyone else. I wouldn't wish it on anyone else. It was very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't have any other questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton. I take it there's no associate exhibit for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Talovic, you will be further asked by Mr. Karadzic on -- by way of his cross-examination. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Talovic.

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were the president of Glogova local commune. When was that?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: I was the president of the chapter in 1998 -- sorry, 1988, 1989, 1990, and 1991, and my tenure in office somehow came to an end at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So were you the president of the local commune in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, both of us have to wait for the interpretation to finish, otherwise we won't be heard by the interpreters. In your 2000 statement, which is 1D4078, on page 2 you say that in early 1992, tensions rose between ethnic groups, and you added that you remember when Bosnia separated from Yugoslavia, the life changed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to read it in English: [In English] "In early 1992, we could feel changes and tensions between the ethnic groups. I remember that when Bosnia separated from Yugoslavia, life changed."

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: That's not what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. We didn't hear the translation of what you said after citing the passage in his written statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's why I asked the witness to wait for the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you look at the transcript, when it stops you will know when the translation is over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you switch from English to B/C/S, you should wait yourself for some time. Yes. Could you repeat your question, the last part of your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question was: Are you establishing a connection between the tensions and the separation of Bosnia from Yugoslavia? Do you think that there is a link between the ethnic tensions and the secession? Would you believe that the situation would have been different, that there were no -- would have been no tensions had there been no separation?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: I was not involved in separation at all, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you did say this, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Now could you answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't separate anything, neither Yugoslavia nor Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I am not attacking you in any way whatsoever. You said that tensions occurred in early 1992. I'm asking you whether the reason for that was the secession or something else.

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: You know that better than I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that in April the army came to Bratunac and tried to seize the draft records from the municipal building, from the draft office. As a result, people gathered in front of the municipal building, you were there, and the army was prevented from taking these records; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the army try to do something illegal, or was it their legal duty and obligation to take hold of draft records?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But this did not take place in April. That was on the 30th of August, 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to tell you how it all happened. A military unit arrives on the 31st of August, 1991, in order to take over the records in order to be able to call up the conscripts. The Muslim crowd gets together in order to try and prevent them from doing so, but the police prevented any major riots. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How was it then?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they wanted to take all these record cards, although the majority -- the minority of officers were Muslims. They could have used those cards for later purposes of killing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you saying and alleging then that on the 30th of August, the JNA wanted to get hold of draft records in order to kill the prominent Muslims? Is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not claiming anything of the sort. I experienced that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On that same occasion, a large group of Muslims gathered around the municipal building and prevented the army from doing that, whereas a group of extremists were breaking things around the town and shooting at the police station; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Talovic, could I remind you again that it's necessary for the benefit of the Chamber and others who follow the interpretation for you to put a pause before you start answering the question, please. And, Mr. Karadzic, what occasion are we talking about now? Is it -- we are talking about April or August?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This event happened on the 30th of August, two or three days after Mr. Izetbegovic withdrew his support of a historic agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, in his amalgamated statement, para 12 he's specifically referring to early 1992, and he said on April 1992. Then you have to explore with the witness first whether it's August or April, and then you should proceed. You should not take it for granted that it should have taken place in August. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I was about to make the point that August is only on the basis of evidence Dr. Karadzic has just given and nothing else. That wasn't what the witness had said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know when this happened exactly, and we are going to present very strong documents in support of that, but I'm eager to hear what the witness has to say, and I'm putting to him proposition made by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, in September 1991, was the flag of the SDS put on fire in Bratunac? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. In that same month of September, the Serbs in Kravica were threatened and told that their houses would be set alight. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the autumn of 1991, armed Muslims erected roadblocks in your village of Glogova as well as in Sandici. Do you remember those roadblocks?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember roadblocks put up by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You don't remember Muslim roadblocks?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: No. Those were definitely Serb roadblocks erected at the exit point from Kravica towards Sandici and on the other exit towards Repovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter 30180 in e-court. While we're waiting, do you remember that by the end of August there was debate and discussion about a historic Serbian Muslim agreement that envisaged Bosnia remaining in Yugoslavia and the Serbs renouncing the idea of autonomous regions, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall any of that. I was more concerned how to get firewood and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Look at this document. This is a discussion between myself and the then member of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Professor Nikola Koljevic. This is September 1991, three or four days after Izetbegovic's withdrawal from the agreement. But if you don't know anything about that, we're not going to address this issue. Can we have the next page, please. I'm going to read this in Serbia. Koljevic and I are talking, and the subject is the barricades, and Koljevic asks me: "Tell me, what happened in Han Pijesak? Are those people alive? "Karadzic: They are, they are. One was wounded in the hand, one in the leg. There are wounded near Bratunac. There are some barricades. "Koljevic: Mm-hmm near Bratunac. "Karadzic: Yes, and then ours put up barricades at Han Pijesak and made a huge queue. "Koljevic: Yes. "Karadzic: And then I could go up there, but I found -- I tried to find a solution. I found a solution and they made a leaflet and said that this barricade was a warning to the authorities of BH because of the lawlessness that was being tolerated. This should be given to every driver who passed by the barricade as a condition for going through. So it was treated as a warning and not as a bandit-like thing or something, you know. "Koljevic: Yes, yes, yes. "Karadzic: Today, we will clear things with them. I think we have to tell Izetbegovic today that the Muslims already hit the Serbs at several places." And you believe that there were no Muslim erected barricades, whereas this conversation clearly indicates that the Muslims opened fire and that the Serbs responded by erecting barricades in Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: This is all news to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be marked for identification as is the standard practice?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm not sure on what basis at all this can be marked for identification. Is Dr. Karadzic putting it forward on the basis that it's authentic, because the witness didn't confirm one single thing about any aspect of this conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Whether it may be contextually relevant as to his reference to barricade.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't think there's enough there, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to respond, Mr. Karadzic, or Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, gladly. I would like this to be a factual basis, but maybe Mr. Robinson has some procedural matters. As far as the facts are concerned, the tensions did not happen in April 1992, but, rather, the Muslim majority was terrorising Serbs as of September 1991. And this conversation demonstrates that we were intent on telling Izetbegovic that this lawlessness against Serbs must stop. That was the basis for my proposal to have this marked for identification simply because this is the way I treat intercepts as such, but if Mr. Robinson feels that he could add something to this, let's hear him.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If -- if I may. Dr. Karadzic has made the context abundantly clear now, so I would withdraw any concern I might have had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D1642, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: MFI. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 3189, two days later. 30189.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this is the second half that you are aware of. This is a conversation between Momcilo Krajisnik and the man called Trifko, who is on duty at the party headquarters. He's asking whether Mr. Krajisnik as the president of the Assembly was aware of the problems in Bratunac. Krajisnik says: "Tell me, what it is?" And Trifko says: "Well, it's war, brother. Two Muslims have already been killed. Everybody is on the run" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please indicate where he's reading from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where are you reading from?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Fourth stance from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you start again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "War, my brother. Two Muslims already got killed. Well, everybody is up in arms. Two got killed, two are wounded. Barricades were put up by the village of Kravica. These are on the move. It is this conflict that is happening in B probably." He means Bratunac. And then Krajisnik is then asking him: "How was it? Do you know?" And then he then explains. Please look at it. He says that one of the Muslims was questioned and then set free. So there was an attempt on the life of Radojlub Djukanovic, the President of the Executive board, a Serb. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The assassin was arrested and immediately released, and Trifko is confirming that by saying, yes, yes. You don't remember any attempted assassination?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: This is news.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Then the group of Muslims set out towards Kravica and then Kravica put up barricades; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Not correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Can it be admitted on the same basis?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I hear from you, Ms. Edgerton, again.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: On this one, no, Your Honour. We -- there -- there is no context. While I understand the principle that this could have been tendered as an impeachment document, Dr. Karadzic hasn't, in fact, done that at all. He's just read this to the witness and asked the witness confirm anything about it that the witness has absolutely no inkling about. So, no, not this time, I would think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we find no basis to admit this document or even for the purpose of marking for identification through this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Excellency, because I'm not the interlocutor, so I can agree with you on that. Can we have a look at 65 ter 30186.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a conversation on the 4th of September between Zvonko Bajgic from Vlasenica and myself. So it is the fifth or sixth line from above. Bajgic is saying: "I don't know whether you've been on top of things since Friday." Karadzic says: "I know that they shot at the president of the Executive Council. That fellow was arrested and then released." And he says: "Yes." And I say: "Then Muslims were headed to Kravica village. Was their intention to attack or what?" Can we have the next page, please. Bajgic says: "After Friday, the SUP deployed, police in those villages, on those hot spots. So only Serbs were deployed in Kravica." Karadzic says: "Yes." Bajgic says: "Because that is what they demanded. The patrols consisting of both Serbs and Muslims were in Konjevic Polje and in that place over there in Lolici." And a bit further down it says: "After the firing at the president of the Executive Council," and Karadzic says: "All right." That was a pretext for that. They informed you about that, and Karadzic says: "Two men were wounded. All right." And Bajgic says: "Then, after that wounding, this assassination was -- there was an assassination attempt." And Karadzic says: "And were Serbs wounded?" And Bajgic says: "And listen, to keep you abreast of things, you note that an attempt was made to kill him but they did not kill him." I don't have time to put entire conversation to you, but this was a crisis, a huge crisis, and the MUP patrolled hot spots and you don't know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: No, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how we should treat this, Excellencies. Believe me, I would have this admitted, because it directly states that the tensions started earlier on -- or, rather, not tensions, a small-scale war, a local war among the local people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you be more specific how this is related to the evidence of this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, what happened to this witness happened on the 9th of May, but the tensions did not start in April. The tensions started in September, at least. There was gunfire, there were barricades, and all of that had to be calmed down. This was a preparation for what happened. This was a local development. It was not ordered from headquarters. That is the essence of what I've been saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I hear from you again, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It may be relevant to events in Bratunac generally and aspects of the police forces, and on that basis I would have no objection. It may be of some contextual assistance otherwise, but it's certainly not relevant to this witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI D1643, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will have a break for 20 minutes. We will resume at 12 past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Talovic, was your village of Glogova armed before the war?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your statement of 2000, that's 1D4078, on page 2, you said -- I have to read it out in English so that it would be translated more accurately: [In English] "Starting from the 1st of April, 1992, Serb police were walking around Bratunac and villages, including Glogova. They had loudspeakers, and they were asking people to surrender their weapons. They also promise that had if we give our weapons, nothing bad is going to happen to us." [Interpretation] So did the Serb police ask for weapons to be surrendered, and what was surrendered in Glogova?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They asked for the hunting guns that people had, along with permits.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ah-ha. So what do we call this? There weren't automatic weapons that were being distributed by the SDA and other activists?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. That is your information. That never happened in Glogova.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In that same statement on page 2 you say -- again, I'm going to read it out in English so it will be translated correctly: [In English] "I had a hunting rifle that I gave away at the municipality building. I had my pistol with me as well, but they did not want to take it from me. They gave me a receipt for my rifle."

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just for the record, I note it's identical to para 13 of his amalgamated statement. Yes, Mr. Talovic. You said -- or you answered already, that's correct. Yes, I'm sorry. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise to the Trial Chamber and the Office of the Prosecutor. Right now there are going to be some very short witnesses. I confused this witness with the previous witness, so this is the witness who had a pistol. So would you please accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So there were guards, guards in Muslim villages were Muslims and in Serb villages they were Serbs, and there were night guards; right?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There were no guards in villages?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: The Serb police guaranteed our safety and security if we handed over the hunting weapons, as I've already explained, that we had, along with permits, and we had no need to organise guard duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In that same statement -- no. Yes. On page 2 of that same statement, you say: [In English] "I know that the SDA won the majority of seats in Bratunac. I also remember that Nijaz Dubisic, SDA, became the president of municipality. The president of the SDS was Miroslav Deronjic. "A man called Sreten Radic was a member of the SDS. He was very active, and he had some high rank in position of SDS. "I do not know who was the chief of police, but I know that police was divided to Serb and Muslim section. That started to happen in April. We did not have police station in Glogova at all, so all that happened in Bratunac." [Interpretation] Do you agree that Serbs and Muslims were together in the police until April and that the chief was a Muslim and that a Serb was appointed quite late and that this was accompanied with lots of quarreling?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: You know what it was like. I was not a politician. The Muslim policemen left Bratunac. They weren't at the station there at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that even when they divided the police, the Serbs and Muslims remained in the same building but on different floors, and they reached agreement, namely that Serbs would work in Serb villages and Muslims in the Muslim villages but they lived and worked in the same building?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: I have no idea whatsoever about the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But over here you did mention that it had been divided. Can we have a look at 65 ter number 603, 603, page 17 in English, and 13 in Serbian. The English seems to be all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The Serbian one is still upside down though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the 23rd of December, 1991, whereas in Serbian we need the 9th of April, 1992. And I'm going to read it out in -- it's the same collection of minutes. We'll find it. It's page 17 in Serbian as well. Mr. Witness, if this is enlarged a bit, can you see that on the agenda is: "The analysis of the past negotiations with Muslims regarding the division of power within the Bratunac municipality, duration of the process and the setting up of the Serbian police force"? Do you remember that an agreement was reached to constitute two municipality in Bratunac, one Muslim and the other Serbian, and that even there were congratulations exchanged, and that Mrs. Subic, the president of the Socialist Party, attacked Izetbegovic after that for going back or canceling this agreement? Don't you know that there was an agreement reached in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. In that case, apparently I shouldn't tender this into evidence, but if an agreement was reached, would you agree that that was a good starting point for solving the crisis in a peaceful way, that a division was signed and in place, that people -- Muslims went to their communities and Serbs went to their communities, and they would share the same [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: But why were you beating me then?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I can only regret what happened to you, Mr. Witness, but one can see that there was bad blood between you starting from August already, and it has nothing to do with me. I'm asking you if the municipality was divided into two municipalities, would that solve a problem?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: The problem wouldn't be solved in any way, because people had no weapons, and this is what you, Karadzic, brought upon my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's look what you also said in your 2000 statement, which is 4078, page 3. [In English] "I was present when this man called Milutin said that they are going to collect weapons from the nearby Serb village called Gornji Magasici as well. Later on, we found out that it did not happen."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's paragraph 14 of the witness's amalgamated statement, P3188.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would never attack my learned friend, Ms. Edgerton, but the truth is that we are receiving the signed amalgamated statements at the 11th hour, although we do receive drafts somewhat earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How do you know that the Serbs were not disarmed, and how do you know that had the events not been so rapid what their intentions were?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that you know that Magasici hadn't been armed. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Because they were shooting at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then you say on the same page: [In English] "The collection was completed by the evening of that day. They advised villagers to continue with their everyday activities without any fear because we already surrendered our weapons." [Interpretation] Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Witness, do you know that on the 20th of April, Naser Oric sent up an ambush for the Serbian reservists and that 20 volunteers were killed on that occasion, their bodies thrown into the river. Do you recall that incident?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember an event in Hranca on page 3 of this same statement, 1D4078, but maybe inadvertently you gave the wrong date and you said 3rd of April instead of the 3rd of May. Do you agree that it could have been on the 3rd of May?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. What I said in my statement about Sacir and his son did happen on the 3rd of May. And on the 6th of April -- no, sorry. On the 6th of May, Hranca was completely cleansed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I am a bit perplexed, Mr. Talovic. On the 3rd of April, Bosnia and Herzegovina was still in existence. There was joint Presidency and the authorities. How come that nobody was informed about this attack on Hranca on the 3rd of April? Maybe it did happen on the 3rd of May though.

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know all I know that it happened and that Hranca was completely cleansed on the 6th and Glogova on the 9th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: April or May?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: The 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that there was no conflict in Glogova on the 9th of April and, rather, on the 9th of May, and you corrected that in your 2000 statement?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't correct anything. The truth is that it did happen on the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us now look at a video-clip, 1D4079. Can we look at this video-clip, please, 1D4079.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the village of Hranca?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On that day, was there an attack on a JNA column that was withdrawing from Sarajevo and that 12 men were killed on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You know that some people fled Hranca, but you don't know what they fled from and why they fled, and you don't know that a JNA column was attacked while retreating and that 12 people were killed? Are you telling me that you don't know anything about that and that those people who came told you nothing about that?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: It is not true that anyone was killed by the Muslims from Hranca, any members of any ethnic community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at another video which is 1D4080. Were there any Serbs in Hranca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serbian part of Hranca is next to Glogova, 2 kilometres, and next to it is the Muslim part of Hranca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's look how -- look at the Serbian houses in Hranca. Were these Serbian houses destroyed by the JNA or the local Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: The Muslims did not destroy Hranca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you acquainted with the Serbs of Hranca? They are only 2 kilometres from you.

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I went to school with some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you forgotten, or maybe you don't know at all -- let me put it this way: Did you know Judge Goran Zekic?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: I did, formally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was he from Bratunac? He was a deputy representing Bratunac, but he was a judge in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what he did and where he was a judge. This is the first time that I hear of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you forget? Did you omit it intentionally, or maybe you forgot that on the 8th of May, Judge Goran Zekic was killed from an ambush while he was try to find a solution for reconciliation between the Serbs and the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: This is completely new to me, because I had no access to any news on the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But this was on all -- covered by all the media. A Serb judge was killed. You didn't notice that?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have these two video-clips admitted into evidence, Excellencies?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it they are -- they were taken by the Defence team recently, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, there's a basis for us to admit the first one, but what's the purpose of the second one? Witness didn't confirm anything about that video-clip.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we see the devastated Serbian houses, and he alleges that this was not done by the Muslims. At the moment, this village is being reconstructed, and I'm sure that neither the Serbs nor the JNA had burnt it, and the witness says that some of the Muslims of Hranca fled to his village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The event did not happen as it is indicated in the testimony, but, rather, the column was attacked and the Serb houses were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you confirm, Mr. Talovic, that the houses, destroyed houses, were Serbian houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't confirm that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, Mr. Witness: Two-roofed houses are usually Serbs, and those who have four are those belonging to the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: I never paid any attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was that the Serbian Hranca that we saw?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: It could have been Muslim as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I -- I just can't see any basis with respect to the second film, Your Honour. The only evidence that we have about what that film purports to represent comes from Dr. Karadzic's mouth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit only the first one.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1644, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that your village of Glogova is situated on the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road on the right-hand side viewed from Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: There is an asphalt road that goes through Glogova, 4 or 5 kilometres, and Glogova is situated on the -- both sides of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But most of it is on the right-hand side; right?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: I would say the ratio is 60/40, but all of it is -- all of it is the local commune of Glogova.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now have 1D4081. Unfortunately, we don't have the translation yet, but the witness can understand our language. 1D4 -- yes, yes. This is an Official Note from 2003 in which it says that a man came and introduced himself. This name is confidential. And he said that during the war he was Naser Oric's unit in the area of Srebrenica and that he knows about how a number of Serbs had been killed in that area. And he goes on to say, first of all, at the beginning of war in 1992, an ambush was set up on the Srebrenica-Zalazje road in which an MP, Goran Zekic, was killed. It was carried out by Mrki and the son of Redzo Salihovic from Bratunac, and all of this had been ordered by Naser Oric, and he's talking about Zulfo Tursunovic. And towards the bottom he says that in 1992 I was in the village of Sandici, Bratunac municipality, where our forces manned a roadblock on the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road. Our forces means Muslim forces, because he's a Muslim. In May and June - can we have the next page, please - when a vehicle ran into an ambush with some people in it. Milutin Milosevic from the Bratunac police station was taken prisoner. Naser Oric was wounded there, as a result of which Naser Oric tortured Milutin who was wounded. He said that he kicked Milutin and finally shot him dead from a close range. Before he was killed, he was taken to Konjevic Polje where he was tortured, cut with a knife, et cetera. Did you know policeman Milutin Milosevic from the Bratunac police station?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: I knew only a few policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about this capture and murder of this police officer?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: This is something completely new to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now have two pages further. Can we see that part, and let's see whether you've heard of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm actually wondering why we're going down this road with this statement. It's the same type of thing we've dealt with again and again and again. This is unsourced. The type at the first page indicates that it came from the Bratunac MUP, but, in fact, if you look, Your Honour, it looks like it's been photocopied from a book. If there's a question in this related to this witness's evidence, I'd like us to get on with it. I'm just wondering otherwise about the relevance of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I quite agree, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may respond briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You didn't give the time-frame of these events put to the witness, and we have a witness who testified as to his surviving a massacre scene. What relevance does this have to his evidence at all, Mr. Karadzic? What -- before we proceed, what time-frame are we talking about in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This witness, a Muslim, came to Bratunac to provide a statement to the police, and we can find out what his name was, and he speaks of events on the 8th of May. Now, the incident that this witness was affected by was on the 9th of May. And here we can see the developments and the events and incidents between the local Serbs and Muslims, and no one from outside the area in any way had any influence on what was going on locally. They killed each other, and it all started with their setting up barricades and ambushes and with the killing of a Serb judge the previous day. Now, all of this was happening in a relatively small area, and this witness should be aware of it, because these are well-known events, and they were reported in the media. Now, if the witness refuses to know anything about it, that also speaks of something.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know anything about this, and I never heard about it. I didn't hear of any of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you will have less than ten minutes to conclude your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mention a vojvoda, namely that these local Serbs who captured you -- well, first of all, tell me, Witness, sir, when did you build a dugout in Glogova?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't a dugout. It was a brook where we took refuge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Didn't you say that you actually sought refuge underground?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this was below my meadow, some 150 metres further. There were some trees there and some underbrush, and that's where we crawled under and hid there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your statement of 2000, you mention a number of individuals who took part in the events on the critical day. You mentioned some Serbs such as Dragan Stevic, Najdan Mladjenovic, and Momir Nikolic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your first statement, you never even mentioned Momir Nikolic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if there was any need to mention him, because when we were taken to the shopping centre, Momir Nikolic was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you recalled this subsequently in the year 2000 when asked about it by the Prosecution; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I probably mentioned that and maybe it wasn't noted, but it is certain Momir Nikolic was there. There's no doubt about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was Momir Nikolic a man of importance, or was he so irrelevant that you never noticed him? I mean, who was more important, this vojvoda, duke, or Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So how come you recalled a vojvoda and you did not recall Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Well, because Mladjenovic came from Kravica. He talked briefly to Momir, and then they took the five of us aside, and because we couldn't all fit in the car, Mustafa Olic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the names of the persons concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Talovic, interpreters missed the names of the persons you referred to. Could you repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you like me to listen? Okay. So when we were ordered to get into the car there was Mustafa, Sejid Ibisevic and Almaz Talovic. They got into the car, and me, Musan Talovic, and Dzevad, we just stood next to the car because there was no room for us in the car that was headed for Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But somebody actually selected them out; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mladjenovic. He just came up and said, "You, you, you, and you." That's it. Now there were five of us there, the five that I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was Golic important? Did he have an important role then or later on in the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You failed to remember, or perhaps you didn't see Mr. Deronjic at the time in Glogova.

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Well, whether I failed to remember or not, I don't know, but some 20 metres away from us, from the shopping centre, from that road there, there were over 500 Serbs there, and we were all herded there, all of us who were rounded up on that day, and then they were -- well, those who were elected were taken for an execution by the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You didn't see him; correct? You said -- you didn't say that you saw him?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I just know that Momir was there. But Deronjic was certainly the top man there. He must have been there. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But in your statement of 2002, 65 ter 22268 in paragraph 3, you say that you had not -- you did not see him on that day?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if that's what I said, that's how it was. I stand by what I said in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you know how many Serbs from Bratunac were killed in this war?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: That's really a silly question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now briefly take a look at 2135, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just for the record, the witness said at paragraph 8 of P3188, that he did not see Deronjic on the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now please pull up 2135.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Talovic, do you know that 90 per cent of the Serb soldiers of the Bratunac Brigade were killed defending Serb villages?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: That's news to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, take a look at this list. It begins with number 152, and this document ends at the number 487. And then there are some additional names added by hand. So just take a look at this column where it says "Defence, defence, defence, defence." So how many Serbs were killed in Serb villages and how do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see this as a total waste of time. After having hearing from the witness that he had no knowledge, what's the point of continuing such questions? It's time for you to come to a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, who was there on that day? Who among the Serbs were there in Glogova on that day?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Well, all the Serbs from the municipality were there. I don't know how many, but they were all there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mean local Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, there were also some soldiers, as I said, the JNA, and of course the army of the Serbian Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 9th of May the Army of the Serbian Republic did not exist?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know then who was made to shoot at me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, when you were arrested, your pistol was noticed.

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then they confiscated it?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which unit was in Glogova then?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Well, only from what I heard from the media later --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could Dr. Karadzic be asked to give the interpreters a chance to finish interpretation before he ask the next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. You were in the middle of answering the question which unit was in Glogova then, Mr. Talovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only heard on the radio that mention was made of the Novi Sad Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What radio was that, what radio station?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Radio Loznica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you were -- there were some very bad blood there locally from August onwards, and all of that was committed by men locally; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSAN TALOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we -- up until the 9th of May, we just went about our business as normal, and I recall that on the 8th of May I was just busy doing the regular things, toiling the soil and so on. Now, as to who committed the murders, you as Karadzic should know better.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to express my regret, Your Honour, that I was not able and not allowed more time in order to shed more lights on the events there and their causes, and I believe that the integrity of the whole proceedings will be undermined by this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's the matter for the Chamber to be concerned about. Ms. Edgerton, do you have any redirect examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, I don't, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then that concludes your evidence, Mr. Talovic. I appreciate very much that you have travelled to come to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go. Please have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will rise together. There's no point of continuing today given there's only five minutes, Ms. Sutherland. Tomorrow we'll continue at quarter past 2.00 again. The hearing is now adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 23rd day of August, 2011, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.55 p.m.,
